problem:
Suppose we wish to solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

and we take a step of size $Δx$ using the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method. Fill in the blanks to complete the weighted-average formula for the increment and the stage definitions, starting at the point $(x,y).$

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx \\ {y}^{′} & =f(x,y) \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & =f({{field-1}},\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\ {y}_{2}^{′} & =f(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,{{field-2}}) \\ {y}_{3}^{′} & =f(x+Δx,\,{{field-3}})\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c
$$

the increment in $y$ using the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method with step size $Δx$ is computed as the weighted average of four sample slopes:

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the initial point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{1}^{′}=f({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{2}^{′}=f({x}_{2},{y}_{2})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{3}^{′}=f({x}_{3},{y}_{3})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{3},{y}_{3})=(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx).$

All four sample slopes are already computed. So, we just need to find the increment on $y.$

We compute $Δy$ using the Runge-Kutta method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(1+2\cdot 2+2\cdot \frac{9}{4}+\frac{29}{8})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot \frac{105}{8} \\  & =\frac{35}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the completed first row is as given below.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $\frac{9}{4}$ | $\frac{29}{8}$ | $\frac{35}{32}$ |

To get the values of $x$ and $y$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x$ and $Δy$ to $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx \\  & =0+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =1+\frac{35}{32} \\  & =\frac{67}{32}\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these rows to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $\frac{9}{4}$ | $\frac{29}{8}$ | $\frac{35}{32}$ |
| $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{67}{32}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y\,(\frac{1}{2})≈\frac{67}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$
